newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU likely to clear Ciba-Geigy maize-officials.
newsitem.headline: EU likely to clear Ciba-Geigy maize-officials.

text.p: The European Commission is likely to clear on Wednesday Ciba Geigy Ag's gene-modified maize for release on European Union markets, Commission sources said on Tuesday.
Commission officials, who asked not to be named, said three panels of EU scientists had raised no significant concerns about the maize, clearing the way for the European Commission to approve it.

The decision, if confirmed, would ease the risk of increased trade tension between the 15-country EU and the United States, whose farmers have faced difficulties exporting to the bloc after growing their first crops containing the U.S.-cleared, gene-modified maize in this year's harvest.

Officials said European Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard was likely to recommend approval, albeit linked to continued monitoring of maize shipments and releases and, possibly, some as yet unspecified labelling requirement.

Approval would end months of uncertainty about the EU stance on the corn, which was developed by the Swiss chemical company to resist the herbicide glufosinate, commonly marketed as Basta, and to carry the Bt-toxin against corn-borer pests. The maize also carries an antibiotic "marker gene".

EU environment ministers put off a decision on the French-backed proposal in June after officials had failed to reach a deal in earlier committee meetings, leaving the controversial issue to the EU executive.

The European Consumers' Organistation (BEUC) added its voice to those of environmental campaigners last Friday when it urged the Commission to throw out the approval application, citing various fears about the effects of the release.

These related to the modified corn's effects on bacterial resistance to certain antibiotics, to the risk that its release would weaken the effect of the existing, "environmentally friendly" insecticide Bt-toxin, and to the possible increased use of the herbicide glufosinate, BEUC said.
Commission officials refused on Tuesday to release details of findings by EU scientists on animal nutrition, food and pesticides.
